extracted.intended_audience: science communicators, university press officers, journalists, and researchers interested in science communication
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for university press releases about scientific studies, focused on avoiding hype and ensuring accurate translation of journal articles into news-friendly copy. Emphasizes matching claim strength to source, disclosing limitations/COI, and clear specification of study design and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal overreach
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag instances where a press release uses causal language despite observational or correlational evidence. The paper notes that when press releases exaggerated claims, news stories exaggerated 81% of the time, and when press releases improperly extrapolated animal findings to humans the news extrapolated 86% of the time—showing downstream effects of causal overreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalization (animal/cell to humans)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying animal or in vitro findings to humans without justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify sample type clearly (animal, in vitro, human) and avoid implying direct human applicability unless supported by appropriate evidence; improper extrapolation in press releases strongly predicts news-level exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude inflation
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide effect sizes in absolute terms rather than inflated relative claims; avoid overstating the practical importance of statistically significant findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implication leaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Speculative practical applications presented as likely or imminent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not present speculative or tentative implications as firm outcomes. Keep implication language proportional to the evidence and study design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid claims of being the 'first' or uniquely novel unless clearly justified by the literature; contextualize novelty modestly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cherry-picking
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlighting a subset of results to create a stronger narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report major results and relevant null findings; avoid selecting only favorable outcomes that misrepresent the total evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat omission
rubrics_metrics.description: Dropping limitations or major caveats from the original paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include all major caveats and study limitations. The anti-hype standard explicitly requires including major caveats and disclosing study limitations so readers understand uncertainty and boundary conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote inflation
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers' quotes presented or framed as 'groundbreaking' or similarly inflated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inserting or amplifying highly promotional quotes (e.g., 'groundbreaking') or reframing modest author statements as definitive breakthroughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding/COI omission
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to disclose funding sources or conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose conflicts of interest and funding sources in the press release; omission is listed as a common hype mechanism and an anti-hype violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match claim strength to source paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Press release should match the strength of claims in the source paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the language of the press release reflects the evidentiary strength, uncertainty, and claims of the underlying journal article rather than amplifying them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use causal language only when supported
rubrics_metrics.description: Use causal language only when supported (e.g., RCT, mechanistic evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit causal phrasing to situations with appropriate study designs or mechanistic support; explicitly avoid causal wording for correlational studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify sample type
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly state whether the study used animals, in vitro systems, or human participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sample/specimen type explicit so readers and journalists do not implicitly assume human applicability when it is absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide effect sizes in absolute terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Report effects using absolute measures rather than only relative percentages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer absolute risk differences or concrete measures to prevent magnitude inflation; this helps readers accurately gauge practical importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unsubstantiated hype words
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from using sensational descriptors unless the evidence and context justify them; these terms are explicit examples of hype to be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include original article DOI/link
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the DOI or link to the original article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linking to the source allows verification and context; the implicit rubric lists including the original article DOI/link as a pass criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be reproducible/verbatim-safe
rubrics_metrics.description: Could be reproduced verbatim without misleading readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The press release should stand on its own such that quoting it verbatim would not mislead; wording should not rely on omitted caveats or context from the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify study design clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the study design explicit (e.g., RCT, observational, mechanistic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear design description helps journalists and readers assess causality and generalizability; it ties to proper use of causal language and appropriate implication framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include counterfactual framing where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Use counterfactual framing to clarify causal claims when suitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where causal claims are discussed, counterfactual language or framing can clarify what would have happened otherwise, reducing overreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author verification / scientist review
rubrics_metrics.description: Send press releases to original scientists for review and correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An intervention where press officers sent releases to original scientists to check evidence strength, flag causal-correlational mix-ups, and identify missing limitations reduced exaggeration without reducing news pickup—recommended procedural standard.
